title: Artificial Intelligence
overview: The AI topic combines graph search with machine learning. You must use Dijkstra's and A* searches, understand artificial neural networks and deep learning, distinguish supervised/unsupervised/reinforcement learning, and explain the purpose of backpropagation and regression.
syllabusPoints: Represent problems as graphs and use Dijkstra's and A* search algorithms.
Explain the purpose and basic structure of artificial neural networks.
Distinguish machine learning, deep learning and reinforcement learning.
Explain backpropagation of errors and regression methods at syllabus level.

definitions.definition: A set of vertices/nodes connected by edges, often with edge weights representing cost or distance.
A shortest-path method that repeatedly finalises the unvisited node with lowest accumulated distance.
A search using f(n)=g(n)+h(n), combining actual cost from start with a heuristic estimate to goal.
Learning a policy from rewards/penalties following actions.
Propagating output error backward through a neural network to adjust weights.
A method for modelling/predicting a continuous numeric relationship.

sections.title: Graphs as search spaces
content: Nodes represent states/locations and edges possible transitions. Weighted edges let algorithms compare routes by cost, time or distance.

sections.title: Dijkstra's algorithm
content: Start with cost 0 at the source and infinity elsewhere. Repeatedly select the unvisited node with smallest temporary distance, update neighbouring distances if a cheaper path is found, then finalise the selected node. With non-negative edge weights it finds shortest paths.

sections.title: A* search
content: A* evaluates f=g+h. g is exact cost from the start; h is a heuristic estimate of remaining cost. A useful admissible heuristic does not overestimate the true remaining cost, allowing A* to focus toward the goal while retaining shortest-path guarantees under appropriate conditions.

sections.title: Artificial neural networks
content: Artificial neurons combine weighted inputs, apply activation functions and pass outputs forward. Training adjusts weights so network output better matches the desired behaviour. Hidden layers let a network learn intermediate features.

sections.title: Learning types
content: Supervised learning uses labelled targets, e.g. spam/not-spam. Unsupervised learning finds clusters/structure without target labels. Reinforcement learning has an agent choose actions in an environment and learn from rewards/penalties rather than labelled answers for every step.

sections.title: Deep learning, backpropagation and regression
content: Deep learning uses neural networks with multiple layers to learn complex representations. Backpropagation calculates how weights contributed to error and updates them to reduce loss. Regression predicts continuous values/relationships, unlike classification which assigns categories.

examTips: In A*, keep g, h and f in separate columns; the next node is chosen by f, not h alone.
Dijkstra does NOT use a heuristic.
When comparing supervised/unsupervised, mention whether training data contains labels.
commonMistakes: Assuming reinforcement learning needs a correct labelled answer for every action.
Using negative-weight edges with Dijkstra as if no issue exists.
Choosing A* solely by smallest h.
